title: The Shirtmaker of Metzingen: Uniforms, Forced Labour, and the Book the Firm Paid For
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Metzingen, the birth in the linen house
stops.date_confidence: attested; German and English Wikipedia agree on 8 July 1885. The birth house address is not given in any source consulted; town-centre coordinates used.
stops.campa: On the eighth of July a fifth child is born to Heinrich Boss and Luise Muenzenmayer in Metzingen, a Swabian market town of linen looms under the escarpment of the Alb. The house sells linen, embroidery goods and lingerie; the boy grows up between bolts of cloth and a ledger. Thirty kilometres north lies Stuttgart, where Hegel was born, where Steiner will proclaim the threefold order and Itten will teach at the Academy; north of that, at Marbach, Schiller was born in a house this atlas calls the tailor's house. The shop is at the selling end of a trade the whole town lives by.
suggested_refs: The Boss family linen and embroidery shop, Metzingen, address unrecorded

stops.name: Bad Urach, the commercial apprenticeship
stops.date_confidence: year attested in German Wikipedia (leaves the Realschule 1899, three-year commercial apprenticeship at Bad Urach); month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January. English Wikipedia places the merchant training in Metzingen instead. Contradiction unresolved.
stops.campa: He leaves the Realschule in 1899 and is bound apprentice to a merchant house at Bad Urach, eight kilometres east under the same limestone wall, for three years of commercial training: stock, invoice, credit, the handling of goods other men weave. The English account puts this apprenticeship in Metzingen and the German record puts it here, and the two do not agree; neither is struck out. He goes at fourteen and comes back at seventeen. He has learned to sell a garment twenty-five years before he learns to cut one.
suggested_refs: The commercial apprenticeship record at Bad Urach, firm unnamed in reachable sources

stops.name: Metzingen, the Wendler weaving works
stops.date_confidence: year attested in German Wikipedia; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January.
stops.campa: He returns to Metzingen in 1902 for practical experience at the Buntweberei J. J. Wendler, a coloured-weaving works in the town, and stands for the first time inside the process rather than behind the counter. Here thread is dyed before it is woven and pattern is a decision made early. A merchant learns what a bolt costs before it becomes a shirt. The German record names the works and says nothing else: not his function, not his wage, not how long he stays. He is seventeen and has now been inside the trade at both ends, the counter at Bad Urach and the loom here.
suggested_refs: Buntweberei J. J. Wendler, Metzingen

stops.name: Konstanz, the mill on the Bodensee
stops.date_confidence: year given in English Wikipedia; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January. The geography lens dates his military service 1903-1905 and places the mill work after it.
stops.campa: After compulsory military service he takes work at a weaving mill in Konstanz on the Bodensee, at the southern edge of the German lands with Switzerland across the water. The sources name the town and the trade and nothing more: not the mill, not the street, not the year he leaves. He is twenty, unmarried, employed in another man's factory. This is the only stretch of his working life spent outside the district he was born in. Everything that happens after it happens within twenty kilometres of his parents' counter.
suggested_refs: The Konstanz weaving mill, name and site unrecorded in reachable sources

stops.name: Metzingen, taking over his parents' shop
stops.date_confidence: year attested in English Wikipedia; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January. Shop address unconfirmed in any source consulted.
stops.campa: At twenty-three he takes over the lingerie and dry-goods business his parents have kept, the linen and embroidery trade of a market town, and becomes his own master fifteen years before he becomes a manufacturer. The address is not recorded in any source consulted. He sells cloth and lingerie bought in from other makers, and manufactures nothing himself. The shop carries him through the war and the inflation, and it is the collateral, the customer list and the standing out of which the factory is later argued into existence.
suggested_refs: The parents' lingerie and dry-goods shop, Metzingen, address unrecorded

stops.name: Metzingen, mobilized and returned at the same rank
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the years 1914 and 1918; the August date is the general mobilization and not a documented individual date. Unit and front are not named in any source consulted.
stops.campa: The mobilization takes him in 1914 as an Obergefreiter, a senior lance-corporal, and four years later the army gives him back at exactly the rank it received him. He rises to nothing. No source consulted names his unit, his front, or one action he was present at; English accounts call him a corporal, which the German record does not support, and say he reached the rank, which it flatly contradicts. The war that decides the whole later shape of his business is one he passes through anonymously, and he comes home in 1918 to a shop, a town and a currency about to fail.
suggested_refs: Wuerttemberg mobilization records, 1914; not consulted

stops.name: Metzingen, the trade in manufactured goods is registered
stops.date_confidence: three-way contradiction, not resolved. German-derived summary: 1922. English Wikipedia: 1923. Company history and both Wikipedias for the factory itself: 1924. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January.
stops.campa: He registers a Gewerbebetrieb fuer Manufakturwaren in Metzingen, a trade in manufactured goods, in the year the mark dies. A loaf costs billions and a registration costs almost nothing. The sources cannot agree when this happens: German summaries give 1922, English Wikipedia gives 1923, and the company's own history dates the workshop to 1924. All three are on the record and none is struck out here. What is not in doubt is that a shopkeeper of thirty-eight decides, at the bottom of the inflation, to turn cloth into garments himself.
sources: HUGO BOSS Group corporate history page
suggested_refs: The Metzingen Gewerbeanmeldung for Manufakturwaren, 1922 or 1923

stops.name: Metzingen, the factory with the Brauchle partners
stops.date_confidence: year attested and used by the company itself for its 2024 centenary; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January. Street address of the first building unconfirmed in any source consulted.
stops.campa: With two partners, Albert and Theodor Brauchle, he opens a factory in Metzingen: shirts, jackets, work clothing, sportswear, raincoats. The street address of the first building is not confirmed anywhere consulted. Thirty kilometres north in Stuttgart, Steiner had proclaimed the threefold social order five years earlier and opened the first Waldorf school that September, and Itten had taught at the Academy there before the Bauhaus called him away. One province is producing a new pedagogy and a small maker of work trousers in the same decade.
sources: HUGO BOSS Group corporate history page
suggested_refs: The first Hugo Boss factory building, Metzingen, address unrecorded

stops.name: Metzingen, shirts of every colour
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction of sequence. Koester establishes only that the firm produced brown shirts early enough for Boss to advertise the fact by the mid-1930s; no year is given for the first coloured-shirt order. Date is a placement, not an attestation.
stops.campa: The workshop takes orders for coloured shirts: red, black, blue, brown. Brown shirts are what the SA wears, and Boss will later swear before a denazification court that these were ordinary civilian orders and that he learned only much later whose shirts they were. Koester finds the firm producing brown shirts early enough that Boss himself advertised the fact within a decade, dating it back to the founding year. The sworn account and the advertisement cannot both be innocent, and in 1946 a court will be asked which of them he meant.
stops.quote: In the ensuing years I received orders for the production of colored shirts, specifically red shirts, black shirts, blue shirts, and brown shirts. They were ordinary civilian orders, in connection with which it was not until much later that I learned that these were party shirts for various political tendencies as well as Catholic youth associations.
stops.quote_source: Hugo F. Boss, statement to the denazification court, 1946, quoted in Roman Koester, Hugo Boss, 1924-1945 (Underwood trans.), p. 18
sources: Roman Koester, Hugo Boss, 1924-1945 (C.H. Beck, 2011; Underwood trans.), p. 18
suggested_refs: Boss's written statement to the Reutlingen Spruchkammer, 1946

stops.name: Metzingen, six sewing machines
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged. The chronology lens dates the insolvency and creditor settlement 1931; the geography lens states sources place it in either 1930 or 1931 and declines to resolve it. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January.
stops.campa: The Depression closes on a small maker of work clothes. The firm goes insolvent and settles with its creditors, reduced by one account to six sewing machines, and the sources place the collapse in 1930 or in 1931 without agreeing. Sales for 1932 will be 38,260 Reichsmarks, the figure of a workshop and not of a factory. He is forty-six and the business he built after the inflation has gone under him. In the April of the settlement year he walks to the local chapter of a party that is not yet in power and takes out a card.
suggested_refs: The Vergleich settlement file, Metzingen, 1930 or 1931

stops.name: Metzingen, membership number 508,889
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the NSDAP membership (1 April 1931). The SS sponsoring membership is tagged [R] in the research pool and carries a year only, 1931, with no month.
stops.campa: On the first of April he joins the NSDAP with membership number 508,889, twenty-two months before Hitler takes the chancellery, and becomes a foerderndes Mitglied of the SS, a sponsor who pays rather than serves. Party clothing orders reach the factory the same year. The family will say afterwards that a drowning business, not conviction, put the card in his pocket; historians point to the SS sponsorship, which no contract required and no customer demanded. Both readings stand in the record and this atlas resolves neither.
sources: Wikipedia citing Lumsden, A Collector's Guide to the Allgemeine-SS, and McNab, Hitler's Elite: The SS 1939-45
suggested_refs: NSDAP membership card 508,889, Berlin Document Center holdings

stops.name: Munich, the black uniform is drawn
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the Diebitsch and Heck design; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January. The location of the SS design office is approximate; the canonical Munich pin is used.
stops.campa: In Munich the SS-Oberfuehrer Karl Diebitsch and the graphic designer Walter Heck draw the black service uniform of the SS. Boss is not in the room. He does not design it, and the legend that he did will outlive every correction; his factory manufactures to a pattern, one contractor among many. The literature on Diebitsch does not mention Hugo Boss at all, so the conflation of maker and designer is never answered, only left unsupported. In this same city five years on, Das Schwarze Korps will denounce Heisenberg as a white Jew.
suggested_refs: Karl Diebitsch and Walter Heck, SS uniform pattern drawings, 1932

stops.name: Metzingen, thirty-eight thousand two hundred and sixty
stops.date_confidence: annual figure for 1932, attested; no month applies, defaulted to 01 January.
stops.campa: Sales for the year stand at 38,260 Reichsmarks. It is the last figure of the small firm and the base against which every later number is read. Within nine years the same factory will book more than 3.3 million, an eighty-six-fold rise, and the difference is uniforms: SA brown, SS black, Hitler Youth, the Reichspost, the Reichsbahn, and in time the Wehrmacht. Nothing about the machines changes and nothing about the workforce changes yet. The customer changes, and the customer is a state that dresses every one of its functions in cloth.
suggested_refs: Company sales ledgers 1932-1941, reproduced in Koester

stops.name: Metzingen, supplier since 1924
stops.date_confidence: advertisement dated ca. 1934 to 1935 in the research pool; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January.
stops.campa: The firm advertises itself as a supplier of NSDAP uniforms since 1924, dating its party work to the year the factory opened. Koester finds the claim an exaggeration, made by Boss to talk the firm up under the Third Reich: the brown shirts were real, the date is stretched backwards to buy seniority. In Berlin the same apparatus that buys these uniforms is preparing the film that will weaponize the name of Joseph Suess Oppenheimer, executed in Stuttgart in 1738, for a country that wants its enemies rendered in costume.
stops.quote: Lieferfirma für N. S. D. A. P. Uniformen seit 1924
stops.quote_source: Hugo Boss company advertisement, Metzingen, ca. 1934; standard English rendering 'supplier for National Socialist uniforms since 1924'. Cf. Koester, Hugo Boss, 1924-1945, p. 18, who notes the 1924 date was an exaggeration. The English string is Wikipedia's rendering, not Koester's wording.
sources: Hugo Boss advertisement ca. 1934, reproduced at wasbishergeschah.at citing Koester 2011
suggested_refs: The ca. 1934 Metzingen advertisement carrying the 'seit 1924' claim

stops.name: Metzingen, Monday to Thursday for seven years
stops.date_confidence: Boss dates the trade-fair years as ending in 1938 in his 1946 statement; the year is his own, month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January.
stops.campa: Seven years of markets and trade fairs, four days of every week on the road with his own goods, his wife and two eldest daughters sewing late and lorries unloaded at night: this is the account Boss gives of how the firm came back from the settlement. It is true and it is incomplete. The same years carry the party contracts that lift sales past a million. In Berlin, Elsa Lindenberg had already been cast out of the Opera in 1933; in Vienna the Gestapo arrests Anna Freud in March 1938. The uniforms go out from Metzingen in every week of it.
stops.quote: Without the tirelessly loyal assistance of my wife and my two eldest daughters, who used to stay up late working, I could never have got my business back on its feet. I and an assistant and even my wife needed to attend trade fairs and markets; in fact, for something like seven years, up until 1938, I was permanently on the go, Monday to Thursday, selling my own goods at such trade fairs and markets. We had to work half the night sometimes, for it was often at night that the lorries had to be unloaded. So it was only through tireless effort that I managed to get back on my feet.
stops.quote_source: Hugo F. Boss, statement to the denazification court, 1946, quoted in Koester, Hugo Boss, 1924-1945, pp. 34-35
suggested_refs: Boss's defence statement to the Reutlingen Spruchkammer, 1946

stops.name: Metzingen, forty French prisoners of war
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month; the geography lens gives October 1940 to April 1941, roughly six months.
stops.campa: From October, forty French prisoners of war are set to work in the factory for roughly six months. Where they were housed, who guarded them and what they were fed are not recorded in any source consulted; the company's own commissioned history does not close the gap either. In Paris that autumn the couture houses are learning to work under occupation. Balenciaga had opened his house there in 1937, and Dior will spend the whole war inside one of them. The clothing industry of Europe is being fitted to this war from both ends at once.
sources: HUGO BOSS Group corporate history page
suggested_refs: Stalag records for the forty French POWs assigned to Metzingen, October 1940

stops.name: Metzingen, three million three hundred thousand
stops.date_confidence: annual figure for 1941, attested; no month applies, defaulted to 01 January.
stops.campa: Annual sales pass 3.3 million Reichsmarks. The factory that booked 38,260 nine years earlier is a war supplier working to quota, and the labour meeting that quota is increasingly not free. The historian Henning Kober describes the firm's wartime managers in two words. Boss himself is fifty-six, a party member of ten years' standing, with a photograph of himself and Hitler on the Obersalzberg hanging in his office. The most profitable decade of his life is exactly the decade in which his state is at war.
stops.quote_source: Historian Henning Kober on the company's wartime managers, cited in English Wikipedia, 'Hugo Boss (businessman)'
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Hugo Boss (businessman)', citing Henning Kober
suggested_refs: Company sales figures for 1941, reproduced in Koester

stops.name: Metzingen, the broken needle
stops.date_confidence: wartime, precise date not given in the source. The year is a placement in sequence and attests nothing; Koester dates the episode only as wartime.
stops.campa: Polish women work the machines under a supervisor named Buchmann. Edith Poller, a German employee, describes him drawing a broken needle out of an injured woman's finger as slowly as he can, grinning; she describes another Polish woman swallowing pins as she sews, trying to die. When Poller objects she is threatened with a concentration camp by the supervisor and by the works manager Hans Schmid, and she adds that Hugo Ferdinand Boss and Eugen Holy were standing beside the men as they spoke.
stops.quote: When a Polish woman was injured he made sure she was not attended to immediately but left to suffer - one had hurt herself, accidentally sticking a needle in her finger; the needle had then broken off. Buchmann pulled out the broken-off bit of needle as slowly as he possibly could, grinning all over his face. One of the Polish women was very upset: she swallowed pins as she worked; she was trying to kill herself.
stops.quote_source: Edith Poller, former Hugo Boss employee, quoted in Koester, Hugo Boss, 1924-1945 (Underwood trans.), p. 59
suggested_refs: Edith Poller's statement, in the Koester study's witness apparatus

stops.name: Auschwitz, Josefa Gisterek taken into the camps
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No source consulted gives the date of her deportation; only that she passed through Auschwitz, Gross-Rosen and Dachau before being returned to Metzingen in March 1943. The date is a placement in sequence and attests nothing.
stops.campa: Josefa Gisterek, a Polish forced labourer at the Metzingen plant, is taken into the camp system and passes through Auschwitz. The date of her deportation is not given anywhere consulted. This is the pin the atlas keeps returning to: Charlotte Bara's music master dies here in October 1944, and Gilles Deleuze's brother does not come back from Birkenau. A woman who sewed uniforms for the German army is inside the machine those uniforms clothed, and the firm that lost her to it will ask for her back.
suggested_refs: Auschwitz prisoner records for Josefa Gisterek, not consulted

stops.name: Gross-Rosen, the second camp
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No source consulted dates the transfer or the length of detention; the date is a placement in sequence only. Coordinates are those of the camp memorial at Rogoznica, Lower Silesia, and are approximate.
stops.campa: From Auschwitz she is moved to Gross-Rosen in Lower Silesia, a granite-quarry camp in the Sudeten foothills that grows into a system of subcamps feeding German industry with labour. Nothing consulted records how long she is held here, what work she is given, or on whose order she is transferred. The atlas marks the pin because a woman on the Metzingen payroll was inside it and because the record of her stops at the bare fact of the transfer. The coordinates are the memorial's and the date is sequence, not evidence.
suggested_refs: Gross-Rosen camp memorial and archive, Rogoznica

stops.name: Dachau, the third camp
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No source consulted dates this internment or its length; the date is a placement in sequence only, immediately before the attested March 1943 return.
stops.campa: The third camp is Dachau, north-west of Munich, the oldest of them, opened in 1933 for the regime's political enemies and grown into a network of subcamps that lends prisoners to German factories. Josefa Gisterek is held here before Hugo Ferdinand Boss has her located and returned to his own plant. Nothing consulted gives the length of the detention or the mechanism by which a private manufacturer retrieves a prisoner from a concentration camp. That the retrieval happened is attested, and it is attested by her sister.
suggested_refs: Dachau prisoner records for Josefa Gisterek, not consulted

stops.name: Metzingen, the camp for the eastern workers
stops.date_confidence: the Ostarbeiterlager is dated 1943 in the source; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January. The interview with Maria Klima is undated beyond the 1990s.
stops.campa: A camp is set up in 1943 for the Ostarbeiter, the eastern workers. Roughly 140 forced labourers pass through the plant across the war, most of them women deported from the Soviet Union and Poland. Maria Klima answers the question about what it was like with three questions of her own. The barracks are not itemized in any source consulted, and the towns these women came from inside the USSR and Poland are recorded nowhere the company's own historian could reach. In Copenhagen that autumn Niels Bohr crosses to Sweden ahead of the round-up.
stops.quote: Have you ever slept in a bed that's been snowed on? Have you ever spent Christmas in a prison camp? Were you ever beaten for picking something up off the ground in order to eat it?
stops.quote_source: Maria Klima, former forced labourer at Hugo Boss, oral history interview, quoted in Koester, Hugo Boss, 1924-1945, p. 57
suggested_refs: The Metzingen Ostarbeiterlager, site unlocated in reachable sources

stops.name: Metzingen, brought back from the camps
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month, March 1943, in Anna Wocka's statement as printed by Koester; day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: She is brought back to Metzingen in March. Her sister Anna Wocka, herself a forced labourer at the plant, gives the entire description the record has kept, in eight words. Boss has recovered a worker from Auschwitz, Gross-Rosen and Dachau and returns her to a sewing machine. The Koester study, commissioned and paid for by the company sixty-eight years afterwards, prints the sentence without softening it, and it is out of the firm's own history that this atlas takes it.
stops.quote: She looked very bad when she was brought back to Metzingen.
stops.quote_source: Anna Wocka, nee Gisterek, former forced labourer, quoted in Koester, Hugo Boss, 1924-1945, p. 60
suggested_refs: Anna Wocka's statement, in the Koester study's witness apparatus

stops.name: Metzingen, the fifth of July
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day in Koester, p. 60.
stops.campa: Forced back to the machines after three camps, ill and with dreadful headaches, allowed a doctor only after much pleading, she faints once after an injection. On the fifth of July she takes her own life. The company's trusty who kept her working while she was already sick is named in her sister's statement only by function, and no source consulted gives him a name. This is the one death in the Metzingen plant's forced-labour record that is carried by name, and it is carried in a book the firm paid for.
stops.quote: The Boss company's trusty made her work although she was already very ill and had dreadful headaches. Only after much pleading was she allowed to visit Dr. Bornhauser. She was so weak she once passed out after an injection.
stops.quote_source: Anna Wocka, nee Gisterek, on her sister Josefa Gisterek, quoted in Koester, Hugo Boss, 1924-1945, p. 60
suggested_refs: Metzingen municipal death record for Josefa Gisterek, 5 July 1943

stops.name: Metzingen, food out of the village gardens
stops.date_confidence: dated 'late 1943 onward' in the source; month is a placement within that range, day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Seamstresses from Neuhausen, Kohlberg, Kappishausern and Dettingen bring food out of their own village gardens into the factory and pass it to the forced labourers on the sly. Edith Poller sits with the Polish women at break and says no colleague ever objected. This happens inside a plant whose managers a historian calls fervent Nazis, under a proprietor carrying a party card, and nobody organizes it. In Rastenburg that September, Mussolini is meeting Hitler at the Wolfsschanze to be told what is left of his war.
stops.quote: We always slipped them some secretly. All our seamstresses from the villages, from places like Neuhausen, Kohlberg, Kappishausern, and Dettingen had their own gardens and always brought food in with them, which would then be distributed on the sly. At break times none of my colleagues ever objected when I sat with the Poles.
stops.quote_source: Edith Poller, former Hugo Boss employee, quoted in Koester, Hugo Boss, 1924-1945, p. 59
suggested_refs: Edith Poller's statement, in the Koester study's witness apparatus

stops.name: Metzingen, what he says about the rations
stops.date_confidence: the claim is dated only 'post-1943' in the source; the year is a placement in sequence and attests nothing.
stops.campa: Boss claims afterwards that the camp catering was muck, beneath human dignity to eat, and that he pushed to have the rations improved. Koester records the claim and records that it cannot be verified, while noting it is consistent with a documented push. This is the shape of nearly everything he says about the war after the war: an act that would exonerate him, attested chiefly by him. In Vichy the year before, Le Corbusier had been working through Ascoral and the Carrel foundation. The professional case for carrying on is made everywhere in these years.
stops.quote: muck ... beneath human dignity to eat
stops.quote_source: Hugo F. Boss on the Ostarbeiterlager catering, quoted in Koester, Hugo Boss, 1924-1945, p. 55; Koester records the claim as unverifiable
suggested_refs: Boss's postwar statements on camp catering, in Koester's apparatus

stops.name: Metzingen, the capitulation and the photograph on the wall
stops.date_confidence: the capitulation is attested to the day. The Fischer testimony about the office photograph is an undated oral history recalling 1945 and is attached here for sequence.
stops.campa: Germany capitulates on the eighth of May and fourteen years of party membership end with the party. Albert Fischer, a Metzingen communist persecuted under the regime, will be the principal accuser at Boss's trial; his son says the photograph of Boss with Hitler on the Obersalzberg was still hanging in the office in 1945, and calls the man an Obernazi. In Darmstadt, Keyserling's school had been strangled by the state in 1933. In Metzingen, the state's supplier is taking a picture down off a wall.
stops.quote_source: Albert Fischer Jr., oral history interview conducted by the Metzingen municipal archives, quoted in Koester, Hugo Boss, 1924-1945, p. 63
suggested_refs: Metzingen municipal archive oral histories on the Boss factory

stops.name: Reutlingen, the decree of the first of March
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; Koester, p. 63, gives the decree of 1 March 1946. The geography lens does not name the town where the tribunal sat; Koester names Reutlingen.
stops.campa: The Spruchkammer at Reutlingen, sitting in the French occupation zone, categorizes Boss as belastet, compromised: an activist, supporter and beneficiary of National Socialism. The decree of the first of March fines him 100,000 Reichsmarks, strips his voting rights and bars him from managerial office for ten years. In Nuremberg that same spring Victoria Ocampo sits in the gallery as the sole Argentine present at the trial of the men whose formations his factory dressed. Fourteen kilometres separate this courtroom from the machines.
stops.quote_source: Reutlingen Spruchkammer, first-trial verdict on Hugo F. Boss, decree of 1 March 1946, quoted in Koester, Hugo Boss, 1924-1945, p. 63
suggested_refs: The Reutlingen Spruchkammer file on Hugo F. Boss, 1946

stops.name: Reutlingen, reduced to fellow traveller
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged. The chronology lens dates the appeal 1947; the geography lens gives a 1946-1948 window without a year. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January. Tagged [R] in the research pool.
stops.campa: On appeal the classification falls from belastet to Mitlaeufer, fellow traveller, the lightest category short of exoneration, and the fine falls from 100,000 to 25,000 Reichsmarks. The business ban is lifted; no source consulted records his voting rights being restored before his death. Maria Klima, who was a forced labourer in his plant, says he was generally taken for a Nazi, and remembers him as sociable with the youngsters. The tribunal has moved him one category down. Nobody has moved the uniforms.
stops.quote_source: Maria Klima, former forced labourer, quoted in Koester, Hugo Boss, 1924-1945, p. 71
suggested_refs: The appeal judgement in the Boss denazification file

stops.name: Metzingen, the firm passes to Eugen Holy
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the handover to son-in-law Eugen Holy; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January. The geography lens adds Boss's son Siegfried as co-owner, tagged [R] and carried by fewer sources.
stops.campa: Because the denazification ban has fallen on Boss personally, ownership and operation pass to his son-in-law Eugen Holy, and by one account to his son Siegfried alongside him. The name over the door does not change. The same building, the same machines, the same works manager who threatened Edith Poller with a camp, and a proprietor who is now legally a fellow traveller with no right to run a company. The firm's continuity through 1945 is total, and its history will not be written for another sixty-three years.
suggested_refs: The 1948 transfer of ownership to Eugen Holy, company register, Metzingen

stops.name: Metzingen, death by tooth abscess
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day and to the place. The geography lens marked the place of death [R] as presumed; German Wikipedia states it flatly, so it is carried here as attested.
stops.campa: On the ninth of August Hugo Ferdinand Boss dies in Metzingen of a tooth abscess turned septic, aged sixty-three, seven months after signing the firm away and a year after the appeal. Penicillin exists in 1948 and does not reach him. Edith Poller, who watched him stand beside the men who threatened her with a camp, calls him an easygoing fellow, by and large; the Reutlingen court called him compromised. Both sentences are on the record. He is buried somewhere in this town and no source consulted says where.
stops.quote: an easygoing fellow, by and large
stops.quote_source: Edith Poller, former Hugo Boss employee, oral history interview, quoted in Koester, Hugo Boss, 1924-1945, p. 61
suggested_refs: Metzingen municipal death register, 9 August 1948

stops.name: Metzingen, the grave no source names
stops.date_confidence: not attested. This is a placement three days after the death, not a funeral date. No source consulted records a burial at all.
stops.campa: The atlas cannot place the grave. German and English Wikipedia are silent on the burial, the Deutsche Biographie entry returns a 404, and the company's own history pages, which narrate the founding, the uniforms, the forced labour and the apology, do not say where the founder lies. This is a gap and it is stated as a gap rather than filled. Metzingen keeps his name on a label sold in every capital in the world, and no reachable source keeps his stone.
sources: Gap: German Wikipedia, English Wikipedia, Deutsche Biographie (deutsche-biographie.de/sfz73374.html, HTTP 404), HUGO BOSS Group history pages, all silent on burial

stops.name: Metzingen, uniforms for the French army
stops.date_confidence: tagged [R] in the research pool. The year is attested for the ownership change and for the postwar reorientation; the month is a placement after the founder's death and attests nothing.
stops.campa: The first postwar contracts are uniforms for the French army and the French Red Cross, then the post office, the railways and the police. The institutional client list of 1943 and the list of 1949 are the same list with the sovereign exchanged. Machines that cut SS black now cut French field cloth for the occupying power that fined the proprietor and barred him from his own company. No retooling is recorded and none is required. A uniform factory cuts to the pattern it is handed.
sources: English Wikipedia synthesis of the company timeline

stops.name: Metzingen, the first men's suits
stops.date_confidence: 1950 for the first order and 1953 for the suits reaching the market are both attested as years; months unknown, defaulted to 01 January. The 1960 move to ready-made is likewise year-only.
stops.campa: In 1950 the firm takes its first order for men's suits, and in 1953 Hugo Boss suits reach the market. The house that will become a byword for tailored menswear begins its actual menswear in the decade after its founder's death, under his son-in-law, in a country rebuilding on other people's credit. By 1960 the suits are made ready to wear rather than in short bespoke runs. The uniform contracts do not stop. They stop being the thing the name is known for.

stops.name: Metzingen, the Holy brothers take the firm out
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January.
stops.campa: Eugen Holy retires and hands the firm to his sons Jochen and Uwe, who take it out of the German-speaking market and into the world. The first fragrance follows in 1984. Everything the name will mean to a customer in Tokyo or Chicago, the black label, the tailoring, the aftershave, is built by the two sons of a Swabian shopkeeper's son-in-law in the thirty years after the shopkeeper's death, on a foundation the customer is never told about and the family has not yet paid anyone to research.
suggested_refs: Hugo Boss company records of the 1967 succession

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the listing
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January.
stops.campa: Hugo Boss goes public on the Frankfurt Stock Exchange. A workshop that booked 38,260 Reichsmarks in 1932 and 3.3 million in 1941 is now a listed company answerable to shareholders, which is also the mechanism that eventually forces the history into the open: a public company can be asked in public what it did. The New York Times and the Los Angeles Times put the question on the fifteenth of August 1997, and the firm confirms the Nazi-era connection fourteen years before it commissions a historian.
sources: New York Times and Los Angeles Times, both 15 August 1997
suggested_refs: The 1985 Frankfurt listing prospectus

stops.name: Radom, production moves east
stops.date_confidence: not attested. No founding date for this site appears in any source consulted; the date is a placement in sequence after the 1985 listing and attests nothing.
stops.campa: Production moves east to Radom in Mazovia, a Polish industrial town a hundred kilometres south of Warsaw. No source consulted gives a founding date for the plant, so the date shown here attests nothing. The labour that sews Hugo Boss garments in Poland at the end of the twentieth century is paid, contracted and free, and it is done in the country from which a share of the plant's wartime forced labourers were deported. The atlas records the coincidence of geography and makes no argument out of it.

stops.name: Izmir, the Aegean plant
stops.date_confidence: not attested. No founding date for this site appears in any source consulted; the date is a placement in sequence and attests nothing.
stops.campa: A second production site is established at Izmir on the Aegean, the old Smyrna, inside a Turkish textile economy that clothes half of Europe by the end of the century. The sources consulted give no founding date at all. What the Metzingen headquarters now does is design, market and account; what it does not do, increasingly, is sew. A town under the Swabian Alb that wove its own cloth becomes an address, a logo and a set of drawings sent somewhere warmer.

stops.name: Morrovalle, the Italian plant
stops.date_confidence: not attested. No founding date appears in any source consulted; the date is a placement in sequence. Coordinates corrected from the research pool's 43.2977, 13.585, which falls about 2.1 km south of the comune centre.
stops.campa: An Italian plant at Morrovalle in the Marche, inland from the Adriatic in the shoemaking country south of Ancona, joins the production map. No founding date appears in anything consulted. The three foreign sites together describe the ordinary arithmetic of European clothing manufacture after 1970: design and margin stay in Germany, stitching goes where labour is cheaper, and the label keeps the name of a Swabian town the garment never passes through.

stops.name: Brooklyn, Ohio, the wage cut and the boycott
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month for the March 2010 boycott. Coordinates corrected: the plant was in Brooklyn, Ohio, a Cleveland suburb, not at Cleveland's Public Square (41.4993, -81.6944), some 7 km away, which the research pool gave.
stops.campa: At the American plant in Brooklyn, a suburb south-west of Cleveland, workers face a thirty-six per cent wage cut and a closure, and the actor Danny Glover joins the boycott in March. A second closure attempt follows in 2015. The English company article names Brooklyn explicitly, while public sources routinely place the plant in Cleveland proper seven kilometres away. The atlas pins the suburb, flags the coordinate it inherited as wrong, and does not present the facility as still operating.

stops.name: Berlin, the foundation initiative
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month, June 2000; day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: In June the company joins the Foundation Initiative of German Business for the compensation of Nazi-era forced labourers, and pays into the fund. Fifty-five years after the capitulation, roughly 140 people and forty French prisoners of war become a line in an accounting. The initiative is collective and no source consulted itemizes the payment by firm. The gesture arrives eleven years before the company will commission anybody to find out in detail what it is paying for, and who.

stops.name: Munich, C. H. Beck publishes Koester
stops.date_confidence: publication month attested as August 2011; day unknown, defaulted to 01. The commissioning year is contradicted: the chronology lens gives 2009, the company's own history page and the afterlife lens give 2011. Unresolved.
stops.campa: Hugo Boss AG commissions the economic historian Roman Koester, through the Gesellschaft fuer Unternehmensgeschichte, to write the firm's Third Reich history with no company involvement in the research or the writing. C. H. Beck publishes it in August as Hugo Boss, 1924-1945: Die Geschichte einer Kleiderfabrik zwischen Weimarer Republik und Drittem Reich. One lens of this research gives 2009 as the year of commissioning and the company's own page gives 2011; the contradiction is recorded and not settled.

stops.name: Metzingen, profound regret
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the BBC report of 21 September 2011. One lens of this research dated the statement 30 August 2011; no source supports that date, and the discrepancy is recorded rather than resolved.
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of September, with the book out, the company issues a statement of regret to those who suffered at the factory run by Hugo Ferdinand Boss under National Socialist rule. One source in this pool dates the statement to the thirtieth of August; the BBC report of the twenty-first is what the atlas follows, and the discrepancy is recorded rather than settled. Every quotation from a forced labourer in this journey comes out of the book the firm paid for, which is the fact governing all of it.

stops.name: London, the GQ awards
stops.date_confidence: month attested as September 2013; day unknown, defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: At the GQ Men of the Year Awards, sponsored by Hugo Boss, the comedian Russell Brand tells the room about the uniforms from the stage. The Koester study is two years old and has changed nothing about what the name means at a black-tie dinner. The history is by now published, corporate and available in English on the company's own website, and it still reaches the public as a scandal delivered by a comic between awards rather than as something the room already knew and had decided how to hold.

stops.name: Metzingen, Holy-Allee and the Outlet City
stops.date_confidence: the renaming is dated December 2023 by the company's history page; day unknown, defaulted to 01. The research pool called 2023 the centenary year: it is not, the firm dates its founding to 1924 and marked the centenary in 2024.
stops.campa: In December the road to the headquarters is renamed Holy-Allee for Uwe and Jochen Holy, ahead of the firm's centenary in 2024. No street in Metzingen is named for Hugo Ferdinand Boss. The old textile quarter around the factory has become the Outlet City, more than eighty discount stores drawing coaches from across Europe to the town where the SS black was cut. The province that gave Hegel and Schiller to Germany now gives it a shopping destination, and the founder's grave is still unlocated.
